title: Roman Kingdom
capsule: The Roman Kingdom was the monarchical phase of early Rome, traditionally dated from the city's foundation (c. 753 BC) through the expulsion of its last king in 509 BC, encompassing a succession of seven kings beginning with Romulus and ending with Tarquinius Superbus. Under kings such as Servius Tullius (578–534 BC), Rome developed its tribal voting assemblies, the Servian constitution, and early circuit walls that would define civic organization for centuries. The seventh king, Tarquinius Superbus, ruled by terror and eliminated senatorial consultation; his son Sextus's assault on the noblewoman Lucretia in 509 BC sparked a patrician revolt led by Lucius Junius Brutus that expelled the Tarquins and installed Rome's first two consuls, inaugurating the Republic. Ancient tradition preserved the king-list in detail, though modern scholarship regards the founding date and early reigns as only partially historical.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The king-list and broad narrative are preserved in Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus but derive from traditions compiled centuries after the fact; no contemporary documents survive for the regal period, and the territorial extent of early Rome is reconstructed from archaeology and later sources with considerable uncertainty.
